claims.text: HfNbTiVAl10 has previously been produced in a hierarchical-heterostructured state with multilevel chemical fluctuations.
A physics-informed multiscale machine-learning framework can directly map experimentally measured hierarchical microstructural descriptors to mechanical properties.
The proposed framework will accurately and efficiently predict Young's modulus, yield strength, and toughness of HfNbTiVAl10.
The surrogate will be a physics-informed neural network using descriptors extracted by rapid imaging or characterization.
The intended application domain is room-temperature tensile and fracture testing at controlled strain rates using routine imaging protocols.
The hierarchical microstructure and its multilevel chemical fluctuations mediate load transfer and deformation behavior.
Embedding physics constraints in the neural network enables mapping from rapid microstructural descriptors to macroscopic mechanical properties.
The descriptor-based neural network reduces reliance on computationally intensive first-principles and CALPHAD calculations.
The proposed method will maintain predictive accuracy while reducing computational demands.
The proposed method is expected to improve prediction accuracy by approximately 20% relative to traditional methods.
The proposed method is expected to reduce calculation time by a factor of 5 to 10 relative to traditional methods.
Conventional first-principles, CALPHAD, and homogenized-input machine-learning approaches typically have prediction errors of approximately 10–15% or more.
Conventional first-principles and CALPHAD approaches require extensive computational resources.
The method may become unreliable when sample microstructures deviate substantially from those represented in the training data.
Extreme compositional variation, aging, or processing anomalies may create out-of-distribution microstructures that reduce reliability.
Insufficient imaging resolution may prevent extraction of the descriptors required for reliable predictions.
Preliminary evidence supports improved accuracy and efficiency.
The magnitude of the accuracy and efficiency gains may depend on the quality and representativeness of the microstructural data.
The hypothesis is falsified if the average prediction deviation for any measured property exceeds 15%.
The hypothesis is falsified if prediction time is not reduced by at least fivefold relative to traditional full-scale simulations.
